title: Inpatient Ward: Patient with a GI Bleed Who Wants to Leave
intro: You are on the internal medicine service. Your next patient is a 55-year-old woman admitted overnight for evaluation of a suspected gastrointestinal bleed after presenting with melena and symptomatic anemia. She is awaiting repeat labs and a possible endoscopy later today. The nurse stops you outside the room and tells you the patient has become increasingly frustrated with the hospitalization, has started removing her monitoring leads, and says she needs to leave to get to work. When she explained that leaving could be dangerous, the patient raised her voice and told her that no one can keep her here. A tech and a second nurse are still in the room after trying to reattach her leads.
goal: Your goal is to reduce the patient’s frustration using appropriate de-escalation strategies, ensure she understands the risks of leaving, and work toward a plan that protects her safety while respecting her autonomy.

actions.desc: Recognize that she has responsibilities outside the hospital and state plainly that the decision is ultimately hers
Ask what is waiting for her at work, whether anyone can be called, and what she is most worried about missing
Describe what an active GI bleed can do, using concrete and non-threatening terms, and check her understanding
Offer concrete options such as expediting labs, contacting the endoscopy team for a time estimate, or arranging a call to her employer
Commit to a specific update time and follow through with what can and cannot be promised
Give reasonable choices such as which tests to prioritize, when to be updated, or whether to speak with the attending directly
Sit down, maintain open posture, let her finish speaking without interruption
Statements such as “You’re in good hands” or “We’ll take care of it” with no specific plan attached
Begin routine questioning without addressing the stated desire to leave
Explain visiting rules, discharge procedures, or unit routines without addressing her concern

actions.type: Tell the patient she cannot leave
actions.desc: Statements such as “You’re not allowed to leave” or “I can’t let you go”
Threaten that leaving AMA means her insurance will not cover the stay or that she will not be allowed back
Statements such as “Your job can wait” or “This is more important than work”
Tell the patient to calm down, or respond in a demanding manner
Describe worst-case outcomes in graphic terms without offering any plan or timeline
Focus on the removed leads or equipment rather than the underlying frustration
Call security, block the doorway, or attempt restraint on a patient with intact capacity who is verbally frustrated
actions.debrief: You moved to keep the patient from leaving by force. A patient with decision-making capacity has the right to leave, even against medical advice, and coercion is not an appropriate substitute for an informed discussion of the risks. The clinical goal is an informed decision — that she understands what an untreated GI bleed can do and what options exist for staying — not a prevented departure.
